sections.body_md:
A real symmetric matrix acts by stretching, not by rotating in a way that creates complex eigenvalues. It has a full set of real eigenvalues, and the eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal. Those directions are the axes of the stretch. In that basis the matrix is diagonal, and each diagonal entry is the factor applied to one axis.

The factorization \(A = U D U^T\) says the same thing in the original coordinates. The factor \(U^T\) writes a vector in the eigenbasis, \(D\) multiplies each coordinate by its eigenvalue, and \(U\) rotates back. Because the columns of \(U\) are orthonormal, the inverse of \(U\) is the transpose. Rebuilding \(A\) is then a sum of rank-one pieces, one per eigenpair: each piece is an eigenvalue times the outer product of a unit eigenvector with itself.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For symmetric \(A\),
\[
A = U D U^T, \qquad U^T U = I, \qquad D = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n).
\]
The trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues, and the determinant equals their product. A nonzero vector \(v\) is an eigenvector when \(Av = \lambda v\). For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - (\mathrm{tr}\, A)\lambda + \det A\). On a positive semidefinite matrix the singular values agree with the eigenvalues.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). The matrix is already diagonal, so the eigenbasis is the coordinate basis. The eigenvalues are 11 and 3. Their sum is the trace, 14, and their product is the determinant, 33.

Check the stretches. \(A(1,0) = 11(1,0)\) and \(A(0,1) = 3(0,1)\). The factorization is trivial: \(U\) is the identity and \(D\) holds 11 and 3. A vector such as \((1,1)\) is not an eigenvector, because \(A(1,1) = (11, 3)\) is not a scalar multiple of \((1,1)\). The two eigenvalues remain 11 and 3.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The identity \(A = U D U^{-1}\) is true for any diagonalizable matrix, but the transpose form needs orthonormal columns. A symmetric matrix can have nonzero off-diagonal entries and still be simple to diagonalize. The diagonal entries are not the eigenvalues unless the matrix is already diagonal. The zero vector satisfies \(A0 = \lambda 0\) for every \(\lambda\), so it is excluded from the definition of an eigenvector. Complex non-real eigenvalues do not occur for real symmetric matrices.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Positive definite matrices are the symmetric matrices whose eigenvalues are all positive, and their quadratic-form level sets are ellipsoids aligned with the eigenvectors. Singular values of a general matrix are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^T A\). The Rayleigh quotient sits between the smallest and largest eigenvalues and equals them at the matching eigenvectors.
